newsitem.title: FRANCE: Euro-MPs approve EU electricity liberalisation.
newsitem.headline: Euro-MPs approve EU electricity liberalisation.

text.p: The European Parliament approved on Wednesday a draft European Union law which paves the way for the partial and gradual liberalisation of the bloc's giant electricity markets.

"This is a historic moment for the development of the European internal market," Energy Commissioner Christos Papoutsis told the EU's directly-elected assembly after Euro-MPs approved the draft directive without amendments.
Papoutsis said he expected EU ministers to rubber stamp the new law next week so that it could come into force in January 1997.

"The European electricity sector will now have a clear framework to base itself on," the Greek Commissioner said, adding that the decision also paved the way for the forthcoming liberalisation of the EU gas market.
"I am very pleased with the results," Belgian Socialist Claude Desama, who has steered the directive through parliament, said after the vote.
The parliament voted on a compromise reached by EU energy ministers last June after six years of wrangling on the controversial issue.
Under the deal by ministers, nearly a quarter of the EU's market will be open to competition from January 1999 at the earliest. This would rise to about a third by 2003.
It was the result of a compromise, mainly between Germany, which pushed for wide liberalisation, and France, wary of any dramatic opening up of markets.

Anxious not to upset the balance and trigger a dispute between parliament and the EU's Council of Ministers which could have prevented the directive getting through at all, Euro-MPs voted not to alter the proposed text on liberalisation.
Left-wing Euro-MPs failed to win enough support to push through changes.

These would have allowed local and regional authorities to negotiate long-term supply contracts with the electricity distributors and forced all EU countries to introduce similar environmental and safety standards in the electricity sector.
Eurelectric, which represents Europe's electricity supply companies, welcomed the result and praised parliament's "responsible attitude".
The Netherlands, which take over the presidency of the EU in January, hope to finalise by July 1997 a draft directive which will introduce competition into the EU gas market.
The draft directives on electricity and gas need the support of both the parliament and EU ministers to become law.
